Dearth

/DURTH/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Dearth means a scarcity or lack of something.

Dearth means a scarcity or lack of something. City council members admitted that the dearth of affordable apartments was quietly pushing young families out of the neighborhoods where they grew up.

Worked Example

When the youth orchestra held spring auditions, forty violinists showed up but not a single oboist. Facing such a dearth of oboe players, the conductor joked that he might have to rewrite the entire symphony around the instruments he actually had.

The orchestra has plenty of some musicians but a serious scarcity of oboists, and that shortage of something needed is exactly what a dearth is.

How Dearth Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scarcity

scarcity: a supply too small to meet the need

paucity

paucity: a smallness of amount or number

lack

lack: the state of being without something

Antonyms

abundance

abundance: a very large, plentiful amount

surplus

surplus: an amount beyond what is needed

How Strong Is It? — shortage → dearth → absence

shortage vs. dearth

shortage vs. dearth: A shortage means there is not quite enough to go around, while a dearth is a serious, noticeable scarcity of something needed.

absence vs. dearth

absence vs. dearth: A dearth means very little of something exists, but an absence means there is none of it at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dear

Root — dear: from Old English deore, precious, costly

Suffix — -th

Suffix — -th: noun-forming ending, a state or condition, as in warmth and growth

Put it together

Put it together: Dearth is the old noun form of dear: the root deore, 'precious, costly,' plus the noun ending -th, the same ending that turns warm into warmth and grow into growth. In medieval England, when food was scarce it became 'dear,' painfully expensive, so dearth came to mean the scarcity itself.

Use the root in a new word: endearing

Use the root in a new word: endearing: The shelter puppy's endearing habit of tilting its head won over the entire staff, and endearing grows from the same root, dear, that centuries ago gave English the word dearth.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Dearth almost always appears in the pattern 'a dearth of' followed by a noun, as in 'a dearth of evidence' or 'a dearth of options.' Despite growing out of the word dear, it has nothing to do with affection today; its natural opposite is a glut or surplus.
